record.question:
A company publishes downloadable reports for global customers. It must block report requests whose source IP addresses are geolocated to countries on a company-maintained denylist, while retaining low-latency delivery elsewhere. The same country policy applies to every report. Reports can be stored in a private S3 bucket.

Which solution meets these requirements with the least operational effort?

options.text: Serve the reports from EC2 instances and maintain country IP ranges as deny rules in the instances’ subnet network ACLs.
Use Route 53 geolocation routing to return no record for denied countries. Serve the reports from a publicly accessible S3 website endpoint.
Use Route 53 geoproximity routing to shift denied-country requests to another AWS Region. Serve the same reports from that Region.
Deliver the reports through CloudFront with a country denylist. Use origin access control and a bucket policy that permits origin access only through the distribution.

explanation.text:
<<4>> combines country-level request filtering at CloudFront with global edge delivery. A private S3 origin with origin access control prevents clients from bypassing that distribution to fetch the same reports directly.

<<1>> requires maintaining changing IP ranges and does not provide a global content cache. <<2>> treats DNS answer selection as authorization; a client can bypass the intended DNS answer and reach the public origin. <<3>> changes routing proximity but does not deny report access.

CloudFront geographic restrictions apply to the entire distribution and depend on IP geolocation. They do not prove a user’s residence or identity; unknown locations and proxies require separate consideration when designing a stricter policy.

AWS documentation (checked 2026-09-18):
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/georestrictions.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/private-content-restricting-access-to-s3.html

diagram_alt: Country authorization occurs on the content request, and a private origin closes the bypass path.

sources.supports: Country allow/deny lists, distribution-wide scope, IP geolocation and origin-bypass considerations.
OAC and a distribution-scoped bucket policy restrict private S3 origin access.

editorial_notes: Replaced overbroad legal-compliance claims with a precise company IP-country policy. Added private origin access; answer ID unchanged.
